root_commitment.why: info binds the root and cannot stop it being minted. HPKE base mode is anonymous -- sealing needs only R_pub, which travels in the package -- so an attacker picks their own auth_root, signs a fabricated history under it, and wraps their own generation key to the GENUINE R_pub. Every signature verifies and the wrap opens. The published substituted-trust-root negative mutates info on existing ciphertext and never attempts this.
root_commitment.digest: RootCommitment = SHA-256( LP("done/pkg-root/v1") || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(hex auth_root) )
root_commitment.sealed: beside R_priv in row 14's envelope, under the same recovery code
root_commitment.checked: recomputed from the manifest and compared BEFORE any generation unwrap

the_attackers_package.note: Internally consistent, and it opens. That is the point: the ciphertext is not the problem, and no amount of checking it helps. Only a value the attacker cannot seal separates this from a real package.

root_commitment.expected: the commitment differs, and the refusal happens before HPKE is exercised at all

construction.one_format: §14.2's cutover package, §14.4's terminal package and §9.3's fidelity archive are one format at §13.5's three lineage states — never-established, live, retired. §14.4 describes the service *populating the portable package* rather than producing a second artifact, and a live package is upgraded to a retired one by importing the terminal record
construction.manifest: Ed25519( assembler ; LP("done/pkg/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(lineage_state) || LP(hex auth_root) || LP(hex lineage_head_digest) || LP(dec epoch) || LP(hex parts_digest) || LP(assembled_by) )
construction.parts_digest: SHA-256( LP("done/pkg-parts/v1") || for each part ASCENDING BY NAME: LP(name) || LP(dec count) || LP(hex digest) ). No separate part count: each part's count is already inside this digest, and a second field would restate it and could disagree with it
parts: checkpoint — row 7’s ciphertext and manifest. **Row 8’s attribution claims are inside it**, because they live in the content root, so there is no attribution part
epochs — enough signed authorization history to resolve credential to capability at any referenced epoch (§14.2 item 2)
suffix — envelopes after the checkpoint, to row 6’s depth
generations — the historical content keys, wrapped (§14.2 item 4)
head — the signed live head, or the signed terminal record (§14.2 item 5, §15 row 9)
recovery — R_pub and the code-sealed R_priv (row 14)

trust_root_anchor.info: LP("done/gen-wrap/v1") || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(hex auth_root) || LP(dec gen), as HPKE base-mode info
trust_root_anchor.why: §14.2 requires the old trust root *bound so it cannot be substituted*. Every other link in the chain is service-signed, so a forger supplying their own root can re-sign all of it; the chain has to terminate in user-held material, and the recovery code is the only such thing. Binding the root in the wrap's `info` means a substituted root opens no generation, so there is no content to re-attribute
trust_root_anchor.why_info_not_aad: `info` is never transmitted. A reader must supply the root it believes rather than read one out of the package, so a wrong belief fails to open instead of failing to match
trust_root_anchor.granularity: Per generation, which §14.1 makes correct rather than convenient: migration rotates to a fresh generation under the new lineage, so pre-migration generations stay anchored to the root that was in force when they were written
trust_root_anchor.never_established: §9.3’s Local archive has no lineage, so both fields are empty and the auth root names the archiving device. Nothing external authenticates it, and §9.3 already says so — the archive answers *does ciphertext still exist*, never *can you decrypt it*

construction.hpke: RFC 9180 base mode, DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256) / HKDF-SHA256 / AES-256-GCM (row 1). Implemented in the generator rather than pinned as a string, because this row’s claim is a binding inside it; it reproduces RFC 9180 A.1.1 on every invocation before it is used

not_here.primitives: SHA-256, HKDF, AES-256-GCM, Ed25519 and X25519 KATs are row 1’s.
not_here.checkpoint: The checkpoint and its manifest are row 7’s.
not_here.attribution: The claims inside the checkpoint are row 8’s.
not_here.recovery_seal: The code-sealed R_priv envelope is row 14’s, unchanged by this row.
not_here.suffix_depth: How deep the suffix part reaches is row 6’s.

k_auth.role: The vanished service's authorization signing key — §14.2's trust root, and the thing this row exists to bind. It also signs a terminal package's own manifest.

forged_root.role: A forger's own authorization key, offered in the trust root's place so the substitution is a value rather than a description.

laptop.role: The restoring credential, which assembles a live cutover package and signs its manifest.

recovery.role: The account recovery keypair. `R_pub` wraps every generation; `R_priv` is what row 14's code opens, and it is where this row's anchor terminates.

vectors.name: live-cutover-package
vectors.why: §14.2’s package: the old service is unreachable and a restoring laptop carries the workspace to a replacement. Everything §14.2 enumerates is a part, and the fifth thing row 9 added — the old lineage’s signed head — is the `head` part.

vectors.name: retired-terminal-package
vectors.why: §14.4’s package, which is the same artifact after the service committed a terminal record: `lineage_state` moves to retired, the `head` part becomes that record, and the service signs the manifest because it is the assembler. Nothing else about the format changes, which is the claim this row makes.

vectors.name: never-established-archive
vectors.why: §9.3’s fidelity archive of a Local workspace, which is §13.5’s third lineage state rather than a fourth artifact. No epochs, no head, no suffix and an empty lineage; the archiving device is the assembler, and **what authenticates it is the code that opens it** rather than any authority, because there is none to appeal to.

truncation_moves_the_parts_digest.why: A real truncation changes a part’s count and therefore the digest that binds it. It is published as a demonstration rather than as an isolating negative because it changes two things at once, and a negative that changes two things tests neither.

must_fail.name: substituted-trust-root
must_fail.mutate: Open a generation wrap while claiming the forger's authorization key as the trust root. **This is the row.** §14.2 requires the root *bound so it cannot be substituted*; binding it in the wrap's HPKE `info` means a substituted root derives a different key schedule and the wrap yields no content key — so a package with rewritten history has nothing to rewrite it over.

must_fail.name: substituted-lineage
must_fail.mutate: Open a generation wrap under another lineage identifier. A migration establishes a new lineage rather than succeeding the old one (§14.1), so a wrap must not carry across one.

must_fail.name: wrap-from-another-workspace
must_fail.mutate: Open a generation wrap as though it belonged to another workspace.

must_fail.name: wrap-of-another-generation
must_fail.mutate: Open generation 3’s wrap claiming generation 2. The binding is per generation because §14.1 rotates forward at migration, so old generations stay anchored to the root in force when they were written.

must_fail.name: retired-presented-as-live
must_fail.mutate: A retired package’s manifest presented with `lineage_state` reading `live`. §14.4 lets an offline replica keep a stale **live** head and forbids it claiming to have observed retirement; hiding a retirement that the package does carry is the same rule pointed the other way.

must_fail.name: substituted-lineage-head
must_fail.mutate: A manifest whose lineage-head digest is changed while everything else stands. This is the field row 9 added to §14.2’s list, and it is what stops a restoring device having to ask a replacement service where the old lineage stood.

must_fail.name: parts-digest-substituted
must_fail.mutate: The parts digest replaced, with no part changed. Isolates the field; the demonstration below is what a real truncation does to it.

must_fail.name: assembled-by-another-credential
must_fail.mutate: A well-formed manifest signed by a different credential. The assembler is named in the message, so this fails on the binding and not only on the key.

must_fail.name: manifest-wrong-workspace
must_fail.mutate: Verify the manifest against another workspace.

must_fail.name: manifest-wrong-lineage
must_fail.mutate: Move the manifest to another lineage.

must_fail.name: manifest-substituted-trust-root
must_fail.mutate: The manifest’s own trust-root field changed. The signature half of the anchor: the wrap makes a substituted root useless, and this makes it detectable before anyone tries.

must_fail.name: manifest-wrong-epoch
must_fail.mutate: Move the manifest to another epoch number.

must_fail.name: manifest-wrong-version
must_fail.mutate: Claim manifest version 2 for a version-1 manifest.

must_fail.name: freshly-minted-package-under-an-attacker-root
must_fail.why: The attack `substituted-trust-root` cannot reach, and the reason this row needed reopening. HPKE base mode is anonymous: the attacker needs only R_pub, which travels in the package. So they pick their own auth_root, sign a fabricated history under it, and wrap their OWN generation key to the GENUINE R_pub with info naming their own root. Every signature verifies, under a root they minted, and the wrap opens -- nothing in the ciphertext is wrong. What refuses it is the root commitment sealed beside R_priv, which the attacker cannot produce without the code.

must_fail.name: attacker-root-refused-before-any-unwrap
must_fail.why: Order, not just outcome. The commitment is checked against the manifest before a single generation is unwrapped, so a package whose root is wrong is refused without exercising HPKE at all. An implementation that unwrapped first and checked afterwards would still have opened attacker-chosen content before noticing.

must_fail.name: root-commitment-for-another-lineage
must_fail.why: The commitment binds all three fields, so a genuine commitment from one lineage does not authenticate a package claiming another.
